Q840951.w: A town near a river mouth on a wide, shallow bay, with large green islands out in the gulf to the north-east.
f: Before 1915 the town was called Ban Don, “village on higher ground”.
The Tapi River shares its name with India's Tapti: the king named the city after Surat, which stands on the Tapti.
Chaiya, north of the city, was an important centre in the era of the Srivijaya kingdom.

q.q: Which island is the classic ferry trip from Surat Thani?

Q748336.t: Cambodia's rice bowl and its bamboo railway
Q748336.s: West of the great Tonlé Sap lake, flat rice paddies stretch almost unbroken, and Battambang stands among them on the winding Sangkae River. Its centre keeps rows of French colonial shophouses. Nearby, locals invented the norry, or bamboo train: a bamboo platform on wheels that rattles along old railway tracks and is simply lifted off by hand when two of them meet.
Q748336.w: A town on a winding river in a vast, flat plain of rice paddies, west of a huge lake.
f: Battambang province is often called Cambodia's rice bowl.
At dusk, huge streams of bats pour out of a cave in Phnom Sampov, a limestone hill south-west of town.

q.q: What is Battambang's “norry”?

Q189133.t: Where the rainforest meets the reef
Q189133.s: Two World Heritage sites meet at Cairns: rainforest-covered ranges rise steeply right behind the town, and offshore the turquoise Coral Sea is scattered with the pale patches of the Great Barrier Reef. The city fills a narrow strip of flat land between them, beside the mudflats and mangroves of Trinity Inlet. On a clear day individual reefs show as lighter shapes in the darker sea.
Q189133.w: A coastal town on a narrow plain between steep, dark green ranges and a turquoise sea with pale reef patches offshore.
f: The Wet Tropics rainforest behind Cairns is among the oldest continuously surviving rainforests on Earth.
The Kuranda Scenic Railway, finished in 1891, climbs from Cairns through the rainforest past waterfalls.

q.q: Which sea does Cairns face?

Q200028.t: New Zealand's biggest inland city, on the Waikato
Q200028.s: The Waikato, New Zealand's longest river, curves through the middle of Hamilton in deep, tree-lined bends, and around the city spread the bright green pastures of the Waikato dairy country. Hamilton is the largest city in New Zealand that does not touch the sea. Small lakes dot the surrounding plain, and Lake Rotoroa lies close to the city centre.
Q200028.w: A city on a broad green plain, split by a winding river, with small lakes around it.
f: The Waikato runs about 425 km from Lake Taupō to the Tasman Sea.
Hamilton Gardens, beside the river, are a series of themed gardens from different eras and cultures.
The Hobbiton film set near Matamata is about 50 km to the east.

q.q: Which river runs through Hamilton?

Q130800.t: Tahiti's harbour town, facing Moorea's jagged peaks
Q130800.s: Tahiti is shaped like a figure eight: a big, round volcanic island joined by a narrow isthmus to a smaller one. Papeete stands on the north-west coast of the larger loop, behind a coral reef that breaks the surf offshore. Across the channel, Moorea's jagged green peaks rise from a turquoise lagoon, while Tahiti's own summit, Mont Orohena, reaches about 2,240 m.
Q130800.w: A town on the north-west coast of a large, round green island, inside a reef; a jagged island lies to the west.
f: Tahiti's two parts, Tahiti Nui and Tahiti Iti, are joined by the Taravao isthmus.
Faa'a airport, just west of Papeete, was built largely on land reclaimed from the lagoon.
Paul Gauguin painted in Tahiti in the 1890s.

q.q: Which island faces Papeete across the channel?

Q612250.t: PNG's port city where the Markham meets the sea
Q612250.s: A broad, grey, braided river — the Markham — spills out of a long, straight valley into the Huon Gulf, and Lae stands on its western side at the mouth. This is Papua New Guinea's main industrial city and busiest port, and the Highlands Highway starts here, climbing inland to the mountain valleys. Steep, cloud-wrapped ranges rise on both sides of the Markham valley.
Q612250.w: A city beside the wide, grey, braided mouth of a river, on a gulf backed by steep green mountains.
f: Lae is Papua New Guinea's second-largest city.
The Markham valley is so flat and straight that the main road from the coast to the Highlands follows it.

q.q: Which river meets the sea at Lae?

Q496442.t: A coal town beside one of the world's biggest pits
Q496442.s: Even from cruise height the Bogatyr mine is hard to miss: a vast terraced pit in the flat steppe, kilometres long, where coal is dug in the open. Ekibastuz grew up around the coalfield in the mid-20th century, and its power stations supply much of Kazakhstan with electricity. One of them, GRES-2, has a chimney about 420 m tall — the tallest in the world.
Q496442.w: A town in flat steppe beside enormous grey, terraced open-pit mines and spoil heaps, with power stations and lakes nearby.
f: The Ekibastuz–Kokshetau power line was built for 1,150 kilovolts, a world-record voltage.
The GRES-2 chimney is taller than the Eiffel Tower.

q.q: Ekibastuz's GRES-2 power station has the world's tallest what?

Q1008853.t: An ore town ringed by giant open pits
Q1008853.s: The flat steppe south-west of Kostanay is pocked with enormous open pits, some of them kilometres across: the iron-ore mines of the Sokolov-Sarbai complex. Rudny was built for them from scratch in the late 1950s, and its name simply means “of ore”. The Tobol River runs past the town, a thin green line through the pale grassland.
Q1008853.w: A planned town in flat steppe beside huge grey-brown open-pit mines and spoil heaps, near a small river.
f: Rudny was founded in 1957 to house the miners of the Sokolov-Sarbai iron-ore complex.
Much of its ore goes by rail to steel mills such as Magnitogorsk in Russia.

q.q: Which river flows past Rudny?

Q133073.t: Edinburgh of the south, on a long fjord-like harbour
Q133073.s: A long, narrow harbour reaches about 20 km inland between steep hills, with the curving Otago Peninsula along one side — and at its head stands Dunedin. Scottish settlers founded it in 1848 and gave it the Gaelic name for Edinburgh. At the peninsula's tip, royal albatrosses nest on Taiaroa Head, one of very few places where albatrosses breed on a mainland.
Q133073.w: A city at the head of a long, narrow harbour between hills, with a hilly peninsula running along its eastern side.
f: Baldwin Street in Dunedin is listed by Guinness World Records as the steepest street in the world.
The University of Otago, founded in 1869, is New Zealand's oldest university.

q.q: Dunedin's name comes from the Gaelic name of which city?

Q41963.t: Sri Lanka's parliament on an island in a lake
Q41963.s: Colombo's sprawl flows east without a break into Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte, the country's legislative capital. Its landmark stands on an island in the Diyawanna lake: the Parliament, designed by Geoffrey Bawa and opened in 1982, with roofs that seem to float above the water. In the 15th century Kotte was the seat of a Sinhalese kingdom, and its long name means “resplendent city of growing victory”.
Q41963.w: Suburbs merging with Colombo to the east, around a lake and green marshes, a few kilometres inland from the coast.
f: Kotte was the capital of a Sinhalese kingdom from the early 15th to the late 16th century.
When the Portuguese reached the island in 1505, Kotte was its leading kingdom's capital.

q.q: Which architect designed Sri Lanka's Parliament in Kotte?

Q203197.t: The last royal capital, in a bowl of green hills
Q203197.s: Tea-green hills fold around Kandy, and the Mahaweli, Sri Lanka's longest river, loops around the town in a wide bend. At the centre is a small lake, created in the early 1800s by the last king of Kandy, beside the Temple of the Tooth, where a tooth of the Buddha is kept. Kandy was the capital of the last independent Sinhalese kingdom until 1815.
Q203197.w: A town in a bowl of green hills, with a small lake at its centre and a big river looping around it.
f: Every year the Esala Perahera procession parades through Kandy with richly dressed elephants.
The Royal Botanic Gardens at Peradeniya fill a loop of the Mahaweli just outside the town.
The Mahaweli, about 335 km long, is Sri Lanka's longest river.

q.q: What relic does Kandy's famous temple keep?

Q11711.t: Gateway to Angkor, between rice fields and a great lake
Q11711.s: North of Siem Reap, the flat green land is marked by perfect rectangles of water: the moat of Angkor Wat, about 1.5 km across, and the West Baray, an 8 km-long reservoir dug by Khmer kings in the 11th century. They are among the few human works of that age you can make out from cruise height. To the south shimmers the Tonlé Sap, the largest lake in Southeast Asia.
Q11711.w: A town south of large, straight-edged rectangles of water in a green plain, with a vast lake to the south.
f: Each wet season the Tonlé Sap River reverses its flow, and the lake swells to several times its dry-season size.
Angkor Wat appears on Cambodia's national flag.

q.q: Which great lake lies south of Siem Reap?

Q7278471.t: Bima's town on a deep, sheltered bay of Sumbawa
Q7278471.s: A long, narrow bay pushes deep into eastern Sumbawa, almost enclosed by dry, brown hills, and at its head lies the city of Bima, with Raba as its eastern, inland district. For centuries this was the seat of the Bima Sultanate, whose palace still stands in town. Far to the west rises Tambora, whose summit collapsed in its eruption of 1815, leaving a caldera about 6 km across.
Q7278471.w: A town at the head of a long, narrow, almost enclosed bay among dry brown hills on the island of Sumbawa.
f: Tambora's caldera, left by the 1815 eruption, is about a kilometre deep.
The palace of the Bima sultans, Asi Mbojo, is now a museum.

q.q: Which volcano, with a caldera about 6 km wide, lies west of Bima?

Q14636.t: A hillside port on Sulawesi's west coast
Q14636.s: Green hills drop steeply to a calm bay on the Makassar Strait, and Parepare, one of South Sulawesi's main ports, climbs them in terraces of houses. Ferries and wooden boats sail from here across the strait to Borneo. The city is also the birthplace of B. J. Habibie, the aircraft engineer who became Indonesia's third president.
Q14636.w: A small city on steep green hills around a sheltered bay on Sulawesi's west coast, facing a wide strait.
f: Habibie, born here in 1936, studied and worked as an aeronautical engineer in Germany.
Makassar is about 150 km to the south by the coast road.

q.q: Which Indonesian president was born in Parepare?

Q497793.t: A gold-rush city of grand buildings and a giant dragon
Q497793.s: Gold was found here in 1851, and within a few years Bendigo was one of the richest gold towns in the world, with grand Victorian buildings to prove it. Shafts went down more than a kilometre into the quartz reefs. Around the city, dry box-ironbark forest and farmland roll away in muted greens and browns, still scarred in places by old diggings.
Q497793.w: A city in muted green-brown country of open forest and farmland, with old mine heaps around it.
f: The Golden Dragon Museum holds Sun Loong, said to be the longest imperial processional dragon in the world.
The town took its name from a local shepherd nicknamed Bendigo after an English boxer.

q.q: Bendigo's name goes back to the nickname of…?

Q595542.t: A town of canals on a vast, shallow estuary
Q595542.s: Just behind the coast south of Perth, the sea floods inland into a huge, shallow lagoon system, the Peel Inlet and Harvey Estuary, often said to be about twice the size of Sydney Harbour. Mandurah spreads around its narrow mouth, laced with canal estates. Dolphins swim right into town, and in summer the estuary is famous for its blue swimmer crabs.
Q595542.w: A town around the narrow mouth of a huge, shallow, lagoon-like estuary just behind the coast, south of Perth.
f: The Dawesville Channel, cut in 1994, gives the estuary a second opening to the sea.
Mandurah is about 70 km south of Perth.

q.q: What is Mandurah's estuary system called?

Q488987.t: A Caspian port in an amphitheatre of desert hills
Q488987.s: Bare, rust-coloured hills curve around a bay of the Caspian Sea, and Türkmenbaşy fills the strip of shore at their foot. Founded by the Russians in 1869 as Krasnovodsk, it became the western end of the Trans-Caspian Railway and the ferry gateway to Baku across the sea. Long, pale sand spits close off the bay to the south.
Q488987.w: A port town on a narrow shore beneath bare reddish hills, on a Caspian bay enclosed by long sand spits.
f: The town was renamed Türkmenbaşy in 1993.
Krasnovodsk Bay is an important wintering ground for waterbirds.
Ferries cross the Caspian from here to Baku, about 300 km to the west.

q.q: Which sea does Türkmenbaşy face?

Q182378.t: Malaysia's planned capital around an artificial lake
Q182378.s: Putrajaya was carved out of oil-palm plantations in the 1990s, and its plan is unmistakable: a long, straight boulevard through the centre and an artificial lake winding around it in green, branching arms. Malaysia's government moved most of its ministries here from Kuala Lumpur, about 25 km to the north. A pink-domed mosque stands on the lakeshore.
Q182378.w: A planned town with a long, straight central boulevard and a branching artificial lake, among green hills south of Kuala Lumpur.
f: The city is named after Tunku Abdul Rahman Putra, Malaysia's first prime minister.
Government offices began moving here from Kuala Lumpur in 1999.

q.q: Who is Putrajaya named after?

Q606162.t: Australia's beef capital, right on the Tropic of Capricorn
Q606162.s: The Tropic of Capricorn runs straight through Rockhampton, so the city stands exactly on the edge of the tropics. The broad, brown Fitzroy River loops through it on the last stretch to the sea, and the forested ridge of Mount Archer rises to the north-east. Cattle country spreads inland, and the city calls itself the Beef Capital of Australia, with bull statues dotting its streets.
Q606162.w: A city on a broad river near its mouth, with a forested ridge to the north-east and wide cattle country inland.
f: By catchment area, the Fitzroy is the largest of all rivers flowing into the Great Barrier Reef lagoon.
Great Keppel and the other Keppel islands lie offshore, about 50 km to the east.

q.q: Rockhampton calls itself Australia's capital of what?

Q3056359.t: Belitung's tin town, among turquoise mining lakes
Q3056359.s: Belitung looks freckled from above: across the flat green island, old tin-mining pits have filled with water and glow turquoise and milky white. Tanjung Pandan, the main town, stands on the west coast by a river mouth. Tin was mined here for centuries, and the island's beaches are scattered with huge, smooth granite boulders, some the size of houses.
Q3056359.w: A town on the west coast of a flat green island dotted with bright turquoise and white pools of old mines.
f: The novel and film Laskar Pelangi, “The Rainbow Troops”, made Belitung famous across Indonesia.
Belitung became a UNESCO Global Geopark in 2021.

q.q: Which metal was mined on Belitung for centuries?

Q1017362.t: A highland town in the broad Wahgi Valley
Q1017362.s: Deep in the highlands of Papua New Guinea, more than 1,500 m up, the Wahgi Valley opens wide and flat between forested ranges, patched with coffee gardens and smallholdings. Mount Hagen is its main town, named after an extinct volcano of almost 3,800 m to the north-west. Every August the Mount Hagen Show gathers clans in feathers and face paint for one of the country's great cultural festivals.
Q1017362.w: A town on a broad, flat, green highland valley floor between steep forested ranges, with a big volcanic massif to the north-west.
f: The town and the mountain are named after Curt von Hagen, a German colonial official of the 1890s.
The Wahgi Valley is one of Papua New Guinea's main coffee-growing areas.

q.q: Which highland valley is Mount Hagen in?

Q203380.t: An Art Deco seaside town on Hawke Bay
Q203380.s: Napier's centre was rebuilt almost all at once in the early 1930s, in the style of the day, and it is now one of the most complete Art Deco towns in the world. It faces the long, grey-shingle curve of Hawke Bay, with Bluff Hill at its northern end. Inland, the plains of Hawke's Bay are a patchwork of vineyards and orchards.
Q203380.w: A coastal town at the northern end of a long, curving bay, below a hill, with green plains of vineyards inland.
f: Cape Kidnappers, at the southern end of the bay, has a large gannet colony on its cliffs.
Captain Cook named Cape Kidnappers in 1769.
Every February the town holds an Art Deco festival, with vintage cars and 1930s costume.

q.q: Which architectural style is Napier famous for?

Q498192.t: Highland town of coffee and the Asaro Mudmen
Q498192.s: A long airstrip runs right through the middle of Goroka, a highland town at about 1,600 m in a grassy valley ringed by forested mountains. Coffee gardens cover the slopes around it. Nearby, in the Asaro valley, the Mudmen perform in ghostly grey clay masks with their bodies smeared in mud — one of the most striking sights of the Goroka Show.
Q498192.w: A town on a grassy highland valley floor with a runway through its middle, ringed by forested mountains.
f: The Goroka Show, held since the 1950s, brings together groups from across the Highlands each September.
Goroka is one of the centres of Papua New Guinea's coffee industry.

q.q: Which group from near Goroka is famous for grey clay masks?

Q580973.t: An orchard town in the shadow of an old volcano
Q580973.s: South-west of Orange the land rises into Mount Canobolas, an extinct volcano almost 1,400 m high that is sometimes dusted with snow in winter. Its rich volcanic soils feed a patchwork of orchards and cool-climate vineyards on the tablelands around the city, which stands at about 860 m. The poet Banjo Paterson, who wrote “Waltzing Matilda”, was born near here in 1864.
Q580973.w: A town on rolling tablelands of orchards and vineyards, with a broad, lone mountain rising to the south-west.
f: Orange was named after Prince William of Orange, later King William II of the Netherlands.
In 1851 gold was found at Ophir, north of Orange — one of Australia's first payable goldfields.

q.q: Which poet of “Waltzing Matilda” was born near Orange?

Q329503.t: A gold town beside a pit you can see from the sky
Q329503.s: Kalgoorlie's Super Pit is one of the few man-made holes you can clearly see from cruise height: an oval of grey, stepped terraces about 3.5 km long and more than 500 m deep, cut into the red earth beside the town. Paddy Hannan found gold here in 1893, starting a rush to the Golden Mile. Around it, dry woodland and salt lakes stretch to every horizon.
Q329503.w: A town in red, dry country beside a huge grey oval open-cut pit, with white salt lakes scattered around.
f: Water reaches Kalgoorlie through a pipeline about 530 km long from near Perth, opened in 1903.
The Golden Mile around the Super Pit has been called the richest square mile on Earth.

q.q: Who found gold at Kalgoorlie in 1893?

Q606335.t: An outback mining city with a smokestack skyline
Q606335.s: Out in the red ranges of north-west Queensland, a tall smelter stack and grey mine workings mark Mount Isa, one of the world's great base-metal mines. A prospector found ore here in 1923, and the town grew on copper, lead, zinc and silver. Its city limits once covered more than 40,000 km², which long made it one of the largest cities in the world by area.
Q606335.w: A town in red, rocky outback ranges beside a large mine with grey spoil heaps and a tall stack, with a reservoir nearby.
f: The lead smelter stack, about 270 m tall, is the tallest structure in Queensland.
The Mount Isa Rodeo, held each August, is one of the biggest in the Southern Hemisphere.

q.q: Which metals made Mount Isa's mine famous?

Q706105.t: A plains city on the Macquarie, with an open-range zoo
Q706105.s: West of the Great Dividing Range the land flattens into the wide wheat and sheep plains of inland New South Wales, and Dubbo stands on the Macquarie River where several highways meet. It is the hub for the whole region. On its edge, the Taronga Western Plains Zoo lets rhinos, giraffes and elephants roam open paddocks that look almost like an African savanna.
Q706105.w: A town on a winding river amid flat plains of large, rectangular paddocks in brown and green.
f: Taronga Western Plains Zoo opened in 1977 as Australia's first open-range zoo.
Old Dubbo Gaol, in use until 1966, is now a museum.

q.q: Which open-range zoo is at Dubbo?

Q230818.t: A green oasis in a high, bare mountain desert
Q230818.s: At about 3,500 m, Leh is one of the highest towns on Earth, and yet the ground here is still more than 7 km below cruise altitude. It is a small green patch where streams run down to the Indus, surrounded by bare brown and ochre mountains in a cold, dry desert. Above the old town, the nine-storey Leh Palace, built in the 17th century, recalls the Potala in Lhasa.
Q230818.w: A small green oasis at the foot of bare brown mountains above the Indus valley, with snowy peaks to the south.
f: Leh's airport, at about 3,250 m, is one of the highest commercial airports in the world.
Stok Kangri, across the Indus to the south, rises to about 6,150 m.

q.q: Which great river flows past Leh?

Q883831.t: Sunny wine town of the Wairau Plains
Q883831.s: The Wairau River braids its way across a wide, flat valley at the top of the South Island, and the plain on either side is ruled into fine stripes by vineyards. Blenheim is the town at the heart of it all — Marlborough, New Zealand's biggest wine region and the home of its famous Sauvignon Blanc. It is regularly one of the sunniest places in the country.
Q883831.w: A town on a wide, flat valley floor patterned with stripes of vineyards, beside a braided river, with hills on both sides.
f: Blenheim takes its name from the Battle of Blenheim, fought in Bavaria in 1704.
Marlborough produces most of New Zealand's wine.

q.q: The region around Blenheim is world-famous for which grape?

Q131233.t: A thread of land between lagoon and open ocean
Q131233.s: South Tarawa is a ribbon of land often only a few hundred metres wide, strung along the southern rim of a triangular atoll, with a turquoise lagoon on one side and the deep blue Pacific on the other. Causeways link its islets into one long, crowded strip. It is the capital of Kiribati, a country whose islands are scattered across thousands of kilometres of ocean.
Q131233.w: A thin, crowded strip of land along the southern edge of a turquoise triangular lagoon, linked by causeways.
f: Kiribati is the only country with territory in all four hemispheres.
Most of the land on Tarawa is only a few metres above sea level.
Tarawa lies about 150 km north of the equator.

q.q: South Tarawa lies just north of which line?

Q605267.t: A windswept port with coral islands offshore
Q605267.s: Southerly winds blow along this stretch of the Western Australian coast so steadily that the river gums near Geraldton grow almost lying down — the famous leaning trees of Greenough. The town curves around Champion Bay, and its port ships grain and iron ore. About 60 km offshore lie the Houtman Abrolhos, low coral islands on some of the southernmost coral reefs in the Indian Ocean.
Q605267.w: A coastal town on a curving bay, with low coral islands scattered far offshore to the west.
f: The Houtman Abrolhos are the heart of Western Australia's rock lobster fishery.
Geraldton is known as one of Australia's best spots for windsurfing and kitesurfing.

q.q: Which island group lies off Geraldton?

Q704257.t: Western Australia's oldest town, on a granite-ringed sound
Q704257.s: Granite headlands curl around King George Sound, sheltering two nearly enclosed harbours, Princess Royal and Oyster, and Albany stands between them. Founded in 1826, three years before Perth, it is the oldest European settlement in Western Australia. Until 1978 it was also home to Australia's last whaling station; today the whales are watched from the cliffs instead.
Q704257.w: A town between two almost enclosed harbours on a wide sound framed by grey granite headlands.
f: Southern right and humpback whales visit King George Sound in winter and spring.
The Natural Bridge and The Gap, granite formations in nearby Torndirrup National Park, face the Southern Ocean.

q.q: Albany's whaling station, Australia's last, closed in which year?

Q12919.t: A ring of coral barely above the waves
Q12919.s: Majuro is a necklace of narrow coral islets around a wide lagoon, joined into one long strip by a single road that runs for tens of kilometres along the rim. Most of it rises only about 3 m above the sea. It is the capital of the Marshall Islands, a nation of 29 atolls and five islands spread across a vast area of the central Pacific.
Q12919.w: A thin ring of green-and-white coral islets around a large turquoise lagoon, with a road along the southern rim.
f: Majuro's road runs for about 50 km, from one end of the atoll to the other.
The Marshall Islands have only about 180 km² of land but nearly 2 million km² of sea.

q.q: Roughly how high does most of Majuro rise above the sea?

Q606169.t: A high tableland town of autumn colours and gorges
Q606169.s: In autumn Armidale's streets turn red and gold: at nearly 1,000 m on the New England Tableland, it is cool enough for European trees. Around it, granite-studded grazing country rolls away until the plateau's eastern edge breaks into deep gorges, where waterfalls drop more than 200 m. For inland Australia, it is unusual: a university town with two cathedrals.
Q606169.w: A town on a high, rolling plateau of pastures and granite outcrops; deep forested gorges cut the land to the east.
f: Wollomombi Falls, east of town, drop more than 200 m and are among the highest in Australia.
The University of New England began in 1938 as Australia's first university college outside a state capital.

q.q: Armidale sits on which tableland?

Q706029.t: A steel town where giant cuttlefish gather
Q706029.s: Red-brown iron country meets the blue-green water of Spencer Gulf at Whyalla, a steel town built on ore railed in from the Middleback Range. Each winter the rocky shallows of nearby Point Lowly host one of the ocean's great spectacles: thousands of giant Australian cuttlefish gather to breed, flashing colours at each other. Nowhere else are they known to gather in such numbers.
Q706029.w: A town on the western shore of a long, blue-green gulf, with red-brown ranges and a steelworks by the water.
f: Iron ore from the Middleback Range has been mined for Whyalla's steel since the early 20th century.
Giant Australian cuttlefish can grow to about half a metre long.

q.q: Which animal gathers in thousands near Whyalla each winter?

Q705705.t: Tasmania's ferry port at the mouth of the Mersey
Q705705.s: On Tasmania's north coast the Mersey River opens into Bass Strait, and Devonport spreads over both of its banks. This is where the Spirit of Tasmania ferries dock after their overnight crossing from the mainland. At the river mouth, the Mersey Bluff lighthouse stands on a rocky headland, and inland, green fields grow on rich, reddish volcanic soil.
Q705705.w: A town on both banks of a river mouth on Tasmania's north coast, facing Bass Strait, with green farmland inland.
f: The Mersey Bluff lighthouse, from 1889, is painted with bold vertical red stripes.
Bass Strait, which the ferries cross, is about 240 km wide.

q.q: Which strait does the ferry from Devonport cross?

Q270734.t: Silver City of the outback, on South Australian time
Q270734.s: A long, grey ridge of mine waste slices through Broken Hill, marking the line of lode — one of the richest silver, lead and zinc orebodies ever found. Around it, red-brown desert plains stretch in every direction. The town is in New South Wales, yet it runs on South Australian time, half an hour behind Sydney, a sign of how closely it has always been tied to Adelaide.
Q270734.w: A town on a red-brown desert plain, with a long grey ridge of mine waste running through its middle.
f: The mining company BHP — Broken Hill Proprietary — was founded here in 1885.
In 2015 Broken Hill became the first whole Australian city on the National Heritage List.
Films such as Mad Max 2 were shot in the desert around the town.

q.q: Which time does Broken Hill keep?

Q1309107.t: Red rocks, salt ponds and ancient rock art
Q1309107.s: Rust-red, rocky hills of the Pilbara run down to a turquoise sea here, and the coast is speckled with the islands of the Dampier Archipelago. Near Karratha, bright white and pink rectangles of salt evaporation ponds stand out sharply against the red. The Burrup Peninsula next door holds one of the largest collections of rock engravings in the world, listed by UNESCO in 2025.
Q1309107.w: A town among rust-red rocky hills by a turquoise sea with islands, beside large white and pink salt ponds.
f: Murujuga, on the Burrup Peninsula, is thought to hold more than a million petroglyphs.
Karratha was built in the late 1960s to house workers for the iron-ore and gas industries.

q.q: The Burrup Peninsula near Karratha is famous for what?

Q271911.t: Assam's capital, tucked into Guwahati's southern hills
Q271911.s: Dispur is less a separate city than a district of Guwahati, spread at the foot of the forested hills that rise towards the Meghalaya plateau to the south. It became the capital of Assam in 1973, after the state's old capital, Shillong, went to the newly created state of Meghalaya. A few kilometres to the north, the broad Brahmaputra sweeps past.
Q271911.w: The southern edge of a big riverside city, where its streets meet green, forested hills.
f: Guwahati, which takes in Dispur, hosts one of the world's largest auctions of CTC tea.
Assam grows about half of all India's tea.

q.q: Before Dispur, which town was Assam's capital?

Q14217100.t: A geometric oasis of irrigated farms in the Riverina
Q14217100.s: On the dry, flat plains of the Riverina, a sudden patchwork of bright green squares and straight canals marks the Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area — and in the middle of it, Griffith. The town was laid out by Walter Burley Griffin, the architect who designed Canberra. Italian migrants, arriving from the 1910s onwards, turned the district into one of Australia's biggest wine-producing areas.
Q14217100.w: A town amid a patchwork of green irrigated squares and straight canals on a vast dry plain, with low hills nearby.
f: Despite the coincidence, Griffith is named after Arthur Griffith, a New South Wales minister, not after its designer.
Water reaches the farms through canals from the Murrumbidgee River.

q.q: Which architect laid out Griffith?

Q550465.t: An iron-ore port of red earth, salt and long trains
Q550465.s: On a flat, red coast fringed with mangroves and tidal flats, Port Hedland is one of the world's biggest bulk export ports, shipping hundreds of millions of tonnes of Pilbara iron ore a year. White salt stockpiles and evaporation ponds glare against the red ground, and ore carriers often wait in line offshore. Trains more than 2 km long bring the ore in from the mines.
Q550465.w: A flat red coastline with mangroves and tidal flats, white salt piles and ponds, and ships anchored offshore.
f: In 2001 a BHP ore train bound for Port Hedland set the record as the longest and heaviest train ever, over 7 km long.
Flatback turtles nest on Port Hedland's beaches every summer.

q.q: What is the main cargo shipped from Port Hedland?

Q1024728.t: Two alpine rivers meet on a green plain
Q1024728.s: Two rivers from the Victorian Alps, the Ovens and the King, meet on a broad green plain, and Wangaratta grew up at their junction. To the south-east the land climbs towards the high country, with the granite plateau of Mount Buffalo on the horizon. The vineyards of nearby Rutherglen and the King Valley make the area a wine destination, and every year the town hosts a well-known jazz festival.
Q1024728.w: A town where two rivers join on a broad green plain, with the foothills of the Alps rising to the south-east.
f: Nearby Rutherglen is famous for its rich fortified muscat wines.
The Wangaratta Festival of Jazz and Blues has been held since 1990.

q.q: Which two rivers meet at Wangaratta?

Q606268.t: A tuna town on a vast natural harbour
Q606268.s: Boston Bay, at the southern tip of the Eyre Peninsula, is a natural harbour often said to be more than three times the size of Sydney Harbour, and Port Lincoln wraps around its shore. Offshore, in circular sea pens, wild-caught southern bluefin tuna are fattened before export. Matthew Flinders named the port in 1802 after his home county of Lincolnshire.
Q606268.w: A town on the shore of a large, sheltered bay at the southern tip of a peninsula, with an island at the bay's mouth.
f: Great white sharks visit the Neptune Islands offshore, and cage-diving trips leave from Port Lincoln.
The Eyre Peninsula behind the town is one of South Australia's main grain-growing regions.

q.q: Which fish is ranched in Port Lincoln's waters?

Q606294.t: Pearls, red cliffs and a staircase to the Moon
Q606294.s: Red pindan earth, white sand and turquoise sea meet sharply at Broome, where Cable Beach runs for about 22 km. The town grew rich on pearl shell, and its pearling luggers once employed divers from Japan, Malaysia and Indonesia. On certain nights from March to October, the full moon rises over the tidal flats of Roebuck Bay and lays a glowing “staircase to the Moon” across them.
Q606294.w: A town on a peninsula of red earth between a long white beach and a broad bay of tidal mudflats.
f: At Gantheaume Point, dinosaur footprints about 130 million years old show in the rocks at very low tide.
Tides at Broome can range up to about 10 m.
Roebuck Bay's mudflats are a major feeding ground for migratory shorebirds.

q.q: What natural show appears over Broome's tidal flats?

Q51678.t: A deep harbour under Rainmaker Mountain
Q51678.s: Pago Pago Harbor cuts almost through the island of Tutuila, a deep, narrow inlet hemmed in by steep green mountains. Above it towers Mount Pioa, nicknamed Rainmaker Mountain for the clouds it traps, which bring frequent heavy rain to the harbour. The town lines the water's edge, and its name is pronounced “Pango Pango”.
Q51678.w: A narrow, deep, green-walled harbour biting into a mountainous island, with a town along its shore.
f: Somerset Maugham's short story “Rain” is set in Pago Pago.
The National Park of American Samoa protects rainforest and coral reefs on Tutuila and nearby islands.
Tuna canning has long been the territory's main industry.

q.q: Which Somerset Maugham story is set in Pago Pago?

Q1663450.t: Victoria's first town, where blue whales feed offshore
Q1663450.s: Portland curves around a wide, calm bay on the far south-western coast of Victoria, and in 1834 it became the colony's first permanent European settlement. To the west the coast turns wild: Cape Bridgewater's cliffs, blowholes and petrified forest face the Southern Ocean. Offshore, cold water welling up from the deep each summer draws blue whales, the largest animals on Earth, to feed.
Q1663450.w: A town on a broad, curving bay, with rugged capes and cliffs to the west and open ocean beyond.
f: The Henty brothers settled here in 1834, a year before Melbourne was founded.
The Bonney Upwelling off this coast makes it one of Australia's few reliable feeding grounds for blue whales.

q.q: What is Portland's place in Victoria's history?

Q642631.t: A long timber jetty reaching into Geographe Bay
Q642631.s: Geographe Bay curves in a long, calm arc of white sand and clear turquoise water, and from Busselton a timber jetty runs out into it for about 1.8 km — the longest timber-piled jetty in the Southern Hemisphere. At its end, an underwater observatory lets visitors see coral and fish around the piles. South of town begins the Margaret River wine region.
Q642631.w: A town on a long, curving bay of white sand and turquoise water, with farmland and forests inland.
f: A small train runs the length of the Busselton Jetty.
The French explorer Nicolas Baudin named the bay after his ship, the Géographe, in 1801.

q.q: Roughly how long is the Busselton Jetty?

Q17980.t: An outback town at the gateway to Nitmiluk's gorges
Q17980.s: On the flat, dry savanna south of Darwin, the Katherine River suddenly drops into a maze of sandstone gorges just north-east of the town that shares its name. Nitmiluk National Park protects thirteen of them, linked by rapids, with cliffs that glow orange at sunset. The town itself is a crossroads, where the Stuart Highway meets the Victoria Highway heading west to the Kimberley.
Q17980.w: A small town on a river in flat, open savanna, with deep, winding sandstone gorges to the north-east.
f: Nitmiluk National Park is owned by the Jawoyn people and managed jointly with the Northern Territory government.
Thermal springs near the town keep their water warm all year round.

q.q: How many gorges make up Nitmiluk (Katherine) Gorge?

Q218768.t: A harbour town inside a flooded volcano
Q218768.s: Rabaul's harbour is the drowned crater of a huge volcano: the sea has flooded a caldera several kilometres across, creating one of the finest natural harbours in the Pacific. Around its rim stand younger cones, and one of them, Tavurvur, still steams and now and then puffs out ash. Much of the town's business has moved to Kokopo, about 20 km along the coast.
Q218768.w: A round, flooded crater bay at the tip of New Britain, ringed by volcanic cones, one of them grey and bare.
f: Simpson Harbour, the port, lies inside the Rabaul caldera, part of Blanche Bay.
Since the 1990s the capital of East New Britain province has been at Kokopo.
Hot springs bubble up along the shore at the foot of Tavurvur.

q.q: What is Rabaul's harbour?

Q154002.t: Palau's quiet capital on the big island of Babeldaob
Q154002.s: On the east coast of Babeldaob, Palau's largest island, green hills and a mangrove-fringed shore surround a small settlement that has been the national capital since 2006. A grand, white, domed capitol complex stands on a hilltop above the sea. Inland lies Lake Ngardok, one of the largest natural freshwater lakes in Micronesia, while the famous Rock Islands are scattered to the south.
Q154002.w: A small settlement on the green east coast of a large, hilly island, with a reef and lagoon offshore.
f: Palau moved its capital from Koror to Melekeok in 2006.
Babeldaob is the second-largest island in Micronesia, after Guam.
The Rock Islands Southern Lagoon is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

q.q: On which island is Melekeok?

Q34126.t: A ring of tiny islets where the runway is a playground
Q34126.s: Funafuti is a loose ring of tiny islets around a lagoon roughly 18 km long, and the main islet, Fongafale, is so narrow in places that the ocean and the lagoon are both in view from one spot. Its airstrip takes up a large part of the land, and when no plane is due, locals use it for football, games and evening strolls. The highest ground is only a few metres above the sea.
Q34126.w: A ring of tiny green islets and reefs around a large lagoon, with one long, thin islet carrying a runway.
f: In 1896–98 the Royal Society drilled deep into Funafuti's coral to test Darwin's theory of how atolls form.
Tuvalu earns a significant income from its internet domain, .tv.

q.q: Which internet domain belongs to Tuvalu?

Q42751.t: Seat of government in Pohnpei's rain-soaked hills
Q42751.s: Pohnpei rises from the sea as a round, mountainous island cloaked in dense rainforest and ringed by a reef and mangroves. Palikir, capital of the Federated States of Micronesia since 1989, lies in the green hills of its north-west, not far from the steep basalt plug of Sokehs Rock. The island's interior is one of the wettest places on Earth, fed by clouds that pile up over its peaks.
Q42751.w: A round, dark green mountainous island inside a ring of reef; the capital lies in the hills of the north-west.
f: Nan Madol, a ruined city of basalt-walled islets off Pohnpei's east coast, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Before 1989 the capital was Kolonia, Pohnpei's main town.

q.q: Which ancient stone city stands on Pohnpei's reef?

Q935006.t: A tiny outback town in a maze of river channels
Q935006.s: Out in Queensland's Channel Country, two rivers, the Thomson and the Barcoo, meet near Windorah to form Cooper Creek, which spreads across the plain in dozens of braided channels. After rain they shine like a web of silver threads, while red sand dunes ripple on either side. Windorah itself is home to only about 150 people, yet its annual yabby races draw a crowd out of all proportion.
Q935006.w: A tiny town on a vast, flat plain crossed by a web of braided river channels, with red sand dunes nearby.
f: In wet years Cooper Creek carries water all the way to Lake Eyre, Australia's lowest point.
Windorah's name is often said to mean “big fish” in a local Aboriginal language.

q.q: Which two rivers join near Windorah to form Cooper Creek?
